claims.claim: In SkillsBench, focused skills with two or three modules did better than comprehensive documentation (arXiv 2602.12670, version 1).
claims.evidence: The v1 abstract (86 tasks, 11 domains, 7 configurations, 7,308 trajectories) states that focused Skills with 2 to 3 modules beat comprehensive documentation. Later versions keep the idea but word it as at most three modules. v4 Appendix F (18 configurations, 87 tasks): 2-3 Skills per task +19.0 pp (43 tasks) vs 4 or more +10.1 pp (21 tasks); comprehensive-size SKILL.md +0.7 pp but only 5 tasks. Those buckets compare different tasks, so they show a pattern, not a controlled test. The Reference correctly labels the figure as version 1; v2 and v3 were not opened.
claims.correct_statement: As a version-1 statement it is correct. For the current version: curated Skills raised average pass rate from 33.9% to 50.5% across 18 configurations; tasks with 2-3 Skills gained about 19 pp versus about 10 pp for 4 or more.

claims.claim: Self-generated skills gave no average benefit in SkillsBench (version 1).
claims.evidence: True of the v1 abstract (no benefit on average). The latest version (v4, June 2026) body reports self-generated Skills below the no-Skills baseline on all three configurations tested: Claude Code with Opus 4.7 -8.1 pp, Codex with GPT-5.5 -11.3 pp, Gemini CLI with Gemini 3.1 Pro -11.5 pp. No pooled figure in the paper; my simple mean is about -11 pp. The v4 abstract page paraphrase did not mention self-generated Skills.
claims.correct_statement: Self-generated Skills lowered pass rate by 8.1 to 11.5 pp on the three configurations tested in the latest version (v4); v1 reported no average benefit.

claims.claim: In Snyk's February 2026 scan of 3,984 public skills, 36.82% had at least one security flaw, 13.4% had a critical issue, and 76 were confirmed malicious.
claims.evidence: Snyk ToxicSkills post (published 2026-02-05): 3,984 skills from ClawHub and skills.sh as of 5 Feb 2026; 36.82% (1,467) at least one security flaw at any severity; 13.4% (534) at least one critical issue; 76 malicious payloads confirmed by human review. The post's headline ('prompt injection in 36%', '1467 malicious payloads') contradicts its own body and table (prompt injection on ClawHub is 2.6%; 1,467 is skills with any flaw).
claims.correct_statement: Wording is faithful. Optionally name the registries (ClawHub and skills.sh) and the 5 Feb 2026 scan date.

claims.claim: According to independent Snyk analysis, 36.8% of available community registry assets contain architectural flaws.
claims.evidence: The number matches (36.82%), but the description does not. Snyk's figure is skills with at least one security flaw of any severity (hardcoded keys, credential handling, third-party content and similar), not 'architectural flaws'; the word 'architectural' does not appear in the post (nearest is 'insecure by design'). It also covers a 3,984-skill snapshot from two registries, not all 'available community registry assets'.
claims.correct_statement: In Snyk's 5 Feb 2026 scan of 3,984 skills from ClawHub and skills.sh, 36.82% had at least one security flaw of any severity, 13.4% had a critical issue, and 76 were confirmed malicious.

claims.claim: Indirect prompt injection: adversarial text hidden inside loaded references read by the model.
claims.evidence: Origin is Greshake et al. 2023 (arXiv 2302.12173, already in the manual's Works Cited): instructions hidden in retrieved content. Snyk's post lists skills that fetch untrusted content, enabling indirect prompt injection, with a four-step chain where the skill author may be blameless. arXiv 2604.02837 names missing separation of data and instructions as a top structural threat for Agent Skills. Scope note: text written directly into a malicious skill by its author is a supply-chain attack rather than 'indirect' injection; 91% of the 76 confirmed malicious skills also used prompt injection.
claims.correct_statement: Keep, but separate two cases: (1) a skill that fetches or loads third-party content carrying hidden instructions (indirect injection); (2) a malicious author putting instructions in the skill itself (supply-chain attack).

claims.claim: Persistent context poisoning: compromised instructions trick an agent into injecting malicious lines into local memory files such as MEMORY.md.
claims.evidence: Snyk's post advises reviewing SOUL.md and MEMORY.md for unauthorized modifications and warns malicious skills can change agent behaviour permanently. Snyk's article (Liran Tal, 3 Feb 2026) says ClawHavoc attackers targeted OpenClaw's SOUL.md and MEMORY.md and describes a staged attack where a first skill plants instructions in memory that fire on a later specific user query. arXiv 2608.03509: 80.0% of skill-mediated attacks survived deletion of the original poisoned records. Scope: the named files are OpenClaw's in Snyk's text.
claims.correct_statement: Say 'for example OpenClaw's SOUL.md and MEMORY.md' rather than a generic 'localized files'; the mechanism applies to any agent that auto-loads a writable memory file.

claims.claim: Conditional backdoors: encrypted payloads stay hidden during static source code analysis, triggering only on specific prompt strings.
claims.evidence: Sources opened support obfuscation (base64 and Unicode to evade detection), skills that look benign at review and change later via remotely fetched content, malicious functionality hidden in auxiliary files, and a staged memory attack that fires on a later specific user query. The fetch reported that explicit conditional/prompt-specific trigger logic and 'encrypted payloads' are not on the Snyk post or article. arXiv 2608.03509 and 2605.11418 describe no trigger-conditioned mechanism. Trigger-conditioned backdoors are documented for model weights (Sleeper Agents, arXiv 2401.05566, not opened), which is a different thing.
claims.correct_statement: Payloads can be obfuscated (base64, Unicode), fetched from attacker servers after review, hidden in auxiliary files, or planted in memory to fire on a later query; pattern-matching scanners can miss these. Drop 'encrypted' and 'only on specific prompt strings' unless a source is added.

claims.claim: Trigger evals: verify similarity loops against 20 queries split 60/40 (train/val).
claims.evidence: Origin is Anthropic's skill-creator skill (public repo and the installed local copy). SKILL.md line 339 says to create 20 eval queries, a mix of should-trigger and should-not-trigger, 8-10 each, with near-miss negatives. scripts/run_loop.py has --holdout default 0.4 (40% of each group held out, 60% train), 3 runs per query, trigger threshold 0.5, up to 5 iterations; the final description is chosen by held-out score. Anthropic's official docs say none of this: they recommend at least three evaluation scenarios, a no-skill baseline, and testing on Haiku, Sonnet and Opus, and say there is no built-in way to run evaluations. 'Similarity loops' is not Anthropic's wording.
claims.correct_statement: Skill-creator's default for tuning a skill description is 20 queries (8-10 should-trigger, 8-10 near-miss should-not-trigger), a 60/40 train/held-out split, 3 runs per query, final description chosen by held-out score. It is a tool default, not a documented Anthropic standard or a validated sample size.

new_findings.finding: arXiv 2609.29454 (24 Sep 2026): 83 smart-contract audit skills, EVMBench, seven agent-model setups, 40 audits each. A skill counts as triggered only when its full SKILL.md is loaded. Activation ranged from 40/40 (Codex with GPT-5.5) to 13/40, 3/40, 1/40 and 0/40 in three setups including Claude with Opus 4.8. Setups with little or no activation showed negligible or negative detection change (three DeepSeek-V4-Pro setups -9.4%, -5.9%, -8.8%); the top setup gained 22.8% detection score and 43.2% captured award. Triggering was driven mainly by the model, not the harness. Scope: one domain; discovery left to the agent with no instruction to use skills.
new_findings.source: Cuifeng Gao et al., Demystifying Agent Skills for Smart Contract Auditing: Design, Effectiveness, Behavioral Impact (preprint)
new_findings.practical_use: Measure triggering from the session trace (full SKILL.md loaded), separately from output quality, and on every model you will use. A skill that works on one model may never fire on another.

new_findings.finding: arXiv 2608.11888 (12 Aug 2026): comparing skill-guided runs with no-skill or matched-skill runs on SkillsBench and SWE-Skills-Bench found 307 skill-induced failures (125 functional, 182 efficiency regressions). Functional failures usually came from skills that look relevant; efficiency regressions were driven by excessive procedure, mainly excessive verification (67 cases) and heavy implementation pipelines (30 cases), not prompt length alone. Introduces the SkillTriage tool. Models not stated in the abstract.
new_findings.source: Gen Dong et al., Agent Skills Can Be Harmful: An Empirical Study of Skill-Induced Failures in LLM Agents (preprint)
new_findings.practical_use: Compare every skill against a no-skill run on both pass rate and cost, and remove mandatory checklists and build recipes the task does not need.

new_findings.finding: arXiv 2605.11418 (12 May 2026): on real ClawHub skills, short text triggers in a skill reached an 86% pairwise win rate and 80% top-10 placement in embedding-based retrieval; description-only framing made agents choose functionally equivalent adversarial variants in 77.6% of paired trials on average; semantic evasion strategies avoided a blocking verdict from the governance check in 36.5% to 100% of cases. No defense described.
new_findings.source: Shoumik Saha et al., Under the Hood of SKILL.md: Semantic Supply-chain Attacks on AI Agent Skill Registry (preprint)
new_findings.practical_use: Do not choose third-party skills by their description or a registry's scan result alone; read the whole skill. Treat your own descriptions as the lever that decides selection and test them with near-miss queries.

new_findings.finding: arXiv 2604.02837 (v1 3 Apr 2026, v2 revised 14 Oct 2026): taxonomy of 7 categories and 19 scenarios across three attack layers and four skill lifecycle phases, mapped onto seven documented incidents. Most severe threats are structural: no clear separation of data and instructions, a single-approval persistent trust model, and capability declarations with no enforcement behind them; the authors say incremental patches will not fix them.
new_findings.source: Zhiyuan Li et al., Towards Secure Agent Skills: Architecture, Threat Taxonomy, and Security Analysis (preprint, revised yesterday)
new_findings.practical_use: Do not rely on a skill's declared permissions or on a one-time install approval. Re-review on every update and keep least privilege in the host settings, not in the skill file.

new_findings.finding: arXiv 2608.03509 (4 Aug 2026, revised 7 Aug): SkillJack poisons agents that turn their own interaction histories into skills. On SkillX a safety detector's catch rate fell from 98.5% on poisoned trajectories to 11.4% on the extracted skills; implanted skills reached attack success of 56.2% (SkillX) and 89.2% (Anything2Skill); 80.0% of skill-mediated attacks still worked after the original poisoned records were deleted. 150 trajectories, four risk categories. Authors argue for provenance tracking; no defense tested.
new_findings.source: Zonghao Ying et al., SkillJack: Persistent Skill Backdoors in Self-Evolving Agents (preprint)
new_findings.practical_use: If skills are generated from your own sessions or documents, keep a note of where each came from, re-read generated skills before keeping them, and delete downstream skills when an upstream source turns out to be poisoned.

new_findings.finding: arXiv 2607.01456 (1 Jul 2026, v2 3 Jul): analysis of 238 real skills gave a taxonomy of 13 higher-level and 44 lower-level components and a best-practice list from 29 sources; their detector found at least one skill smell (a departure from those practices) in over 99% of SKILL.md files, and smells rarely disappear as skills evolve.
new_findings.source: David Boram Hong et al., From Anatomy to Smells: An Empirical Study of SKILL.md in Agent Skills (preprint)
new_findings.practical_use: Run an authoring lint against published best practices on every skill; your skill_audit.py and validate_skill.sh cover some structure checks, so compare them with the Anthropic best-practices checklist.

recommendations: Do not ship skills the model wrote on its own. SkillsBench v4 found self-written skills lowered pass rate by 8.1 to 11.5 pp on three configurations. Draft with AI, measure against a no-skill run, then cut anything that does not close a measured gap.

Compare with and without the skill on both pass rate and cost. Skills that look relevant can cause wrong or missing work, and mandatory verification steps and heavy build recipes cause cost regressions (arXiv 2608.11888).

Keep skills small and few: 2-3 Skills per task did better than 4 or more (+19.0 vs +10.1 pp), and the longest SKILL.md files showed no lift, though that group is only 5 tasks. Your 500-line limit and one-job rule fit this.

Measure triggering from the trace (full SKILL.md loaded), separately from output quality, and per model. One study saw activation from 0/40 to 40/40 across models (arXiv 2609.29454). Add 'per model' and 'from the trace' to master prompt Phase 2.

Treat the 20-query, 60/40 design as skill-creator's default, not a standard: about 12 training and 8 held-out queries is thin, near-miss negatives matter more than count, and results should state runs per query (default 3).

Fix the wording in your documents: Omnibus line 46 (Snyk 36.82% is any security flaw across 3,984 skills in two registries, not 'architectural flaws'), line 48 (MEMORY.md is OpenClaw's in Snyk's text), line 49 (drop 'encrypted payloads' and 'only on specific prompt strings' unless sourced), lines 42 and 59 ('similarity loops' is not Anthropic's term); Reference v1.2 line 29 (add the v4 SkillsBench numbers).

Do your own security pass and treat scanners as a floor. Read every script and reference, pin the reviewed version, and check for fetched remote content, base64 or eval, hidden Unicode and writes to memory files. A keyword search of your two validators found none of these checks (not read in full); adding warnings is cheap but one study saw governance checks evaded in 36.5% to 100% of cases (arXiv 2605.11418).

Be careful with skills built automatically from your own sessions: poison can become a lasting skill that survives deleting the source (arXiv 2608.03509). Record provenance and re-read generated skills. After removing a suspect skill, re-read your memory files.

Quote Snyk from its body and table, not its headline: the headline says prompt injection in 36% and 1,467 malicious payloads, but the table shows 2.6% prompt injection on ClawHub and the malicious count is 76.

checks.reason: The v4 full text (section 5.1.1, read through a summarizing fetch) puts self-generated Skills below the no-Skills baseline on all three configurations: -8.1 pp (Claude Code, Opus 4.7), -11.3 pp (Codex, GPT-5.5), -11.5 pp (Gemini CLI, Gemini 3.1 Pro). The v1 abstract (arXiv 2602.12670v1) says self-generated Skills gave no benefit on average; the one quote used: "Self-generated Skills provide no benefit on average". The proposed correct statement matches both. Not read: the v4 text past character 100,000 of about 175,000, where any pooled figure would sit.

The Snyk post gives 36.82% as 1,467 skills with at least one security flaw, in a table row labelled 'Skills with any security issue', which counts any severity. The denominator is 3,984 skills from ClawHub and skills.sh as of 5 Feb 2026, though a later sentence mentions only ClawHub. 13.4% (534 skills) have a critical issue, and 76 malicious payloads were confirmed. The word 'architectural' does not appear. The finding's parenthetical examples (hardcoded keys and similar) were not checked.

The Snyk post does not mention encrypted payloads, static source code analysis, or triggering only on specific prompt strings. Its only 'encrypted' wording refers to encrypted archive passwords in a list of embedded tokens. It does say base64 or Unicode obfuscation is used to evade detection, that attackers can change behavior later by updating fetched content, and that malicious skills can poison agent memory for persistence. It does not mention auxiliary files or a trigger on a later query. The arXiv 2605.11418 abstract describes no designed trigger, and the 2608.03509 abstract mentions only skills that activate unintentionally on benign queries. Corrected statement: payloads can be obfuscated (base64, Unicode), fetched from attacker servers after review, or used to poison agent memory for persistence, and scanners can miss these. Drop the auxiliary-file and delayed-trigger wording unless a source that states it is cited.

SKILL.md asks for 20 eval queries, a mix of should-trigger and should-not-trigger, 8 to 10 each. Near-miss negatives are called the most valuable ones; that is guidance, not a requirement, so the finding's 'near-miss' wording slightly overstates. It splits 60% train and 40% held-out test and selects the description by test score, not train score. 'Similarity loop' and 'validation' do not appear. scripts/run_loop.py defaults match: holdout 0.4, 3 runs per query, trigger threshold 0.5, max 5 iterations. The official platform.claude.com skill best-practices page recommends at least three evaluation scenarios, a no-skill baseline, and testing with Haiku, Sonnet and Opus. It says there is not currently a built-in way to run these evaluations, and gives no 20-query or 60/40 standard.

Title, first author (Cuifeng Gao) and submission date (24 Sep 2026) match. The abstract gives 83 audit skills, EVMBench, seven agent-model configurations, and the top setup (Codex with GPT-5.5) at +22.8% detection score and +43.2% captured award. The HTML body defines activation as the full SKILL.md being read. Activation: Codex/GPT-5.5 40/40; Gemini-3.5-Flash 13/40; GLM-5.1 3/40; DeepSeek-V4-Pro via OpenCode 1/40; Claude Code with Opus-4.8 0/40. The three DeepSeek setups changed detection by -9.4, -5.9 and -8.8 percent. The body attributes triggering mainly to the model with limited harness effect, but notes that Opus-4.8's 0/40 is unexplained. Corrections: the claim says 'three setups' for four lower activation figures. The 'no instruction to use skills' scope was not checked.

Title, first author (Gen Dong) and submission date (12 Aug 2026) match. The abstract reports 307 skill-induced failures: 125 functional and 182 efficiency regressions, on SkillsBench and SWE-Skills-Bench, compared against no-skill or matched-skill runs. Functional failures come from seemingly relevant skills. Efficiency regressions are led by excessive verification (67 cases) and heavy implementation pipelines (30 cases), and are not explained by prompt length alone. SkillTriage is introduced. The abstract names no models, as the claim says.

Title, first author (Shoumik Saha) and date (12 May 2026) match. The abstract reports up to 86% pairwise win rate and 80% top-10 placement for short text triggers in embedding retrieval, 77.6% of paired trials on average for description-only framing, and 36.5% to 100% of cases where semantic evasion avoided a blocking verdict. The claim's 'reached 86%' drops the 'up to' scope, which should be kept. The abstract has no defense; the full text was not read, so 'no defense described' and 'on real ClawHub skills' are not fully verified.

Title, first author (Zhiyuan Li), v1 date (3 Apr 2026) and one revision (v2, 14 Oct 2026) match. The abstract gives seven categories and nineteen scenarios across three attack layers and four lifecycle phases (Creation, Distribution, Deployment, Execution), with seven documented incidents mapped. The most severe threats are structural: no data-instruction boundary, a single-approval persistent trust model, and capability declarations with no enforcement semantics. The abstract says these cannot be fixed by incremental mitigations alone, which matches the claim in paraphrase. The exact phrase 'no clear separation of data and instructions' does not appear; the wording is equivalent.

Title, first author (Zonghao Ying), v1 date (4 Aug 2026) and v2 (7 Aug 2026) match. The abstract says safety detection drops from 98.5% on poisoned trajectories to 11.4% on extracted skills. The abstract sentence does not name SkillX for that pair, so the 'On SkillX' label is unverified. Attack success is 56.2% and 89.2% on the two systems, with SkillX listed first. 80.0% of skill-mediated attacks persist after the poisoned records are deleted. The dataset is 150 trajectories in four policy-risk categories. The authors propose provenance-aware lifecycle protection; no specific defense is evaluated. The abstract describes no designed trigger that fires on a specific prompt or later query.

Title, first author (David Boram Hong), v1 date (1 Jul 2026) and v2 (3 Jul 2026) match. The abstract reports 238 real-world skills analysed, a taxonomy of 13 higher-level and 44 lower-level components, a multivocal review of 29 sources for best practices, over 99% of SKILL.md files with at least one skill smell, and smells that rarely disappear as skills evolve. The detector's internals were not checked beyond the abstract.

findings.claim: Section 7.3: Anthropic's documentation says a role in the system prompt "focuses Claude's behavior and tone for your use case".
findings.evidence: Anthropic Prompting best practices page, opened 2026-10-15: "Setting a role in the system prompt focuses Claude's behavior and tone for your use case."

findings.claim: Section 7.4: for inputs of about 20K tokens or more, Anthropic advises placing long documents near the top, above query, instructions and examples; queries at the end can improve quality by up to 30 percent in tests; the tests are not published.
findings.evidence: Same page: "(20k+ tokens)", "near the top of your prompt, above your query, instructions, and examples", "Queries at the end can improve response quality by up to 30 percent in tests". The page gives no test details, as the manual says.

findings.claim: Section 7.5: Anthropic says "Tell Claude what to do instead of what not to do", replacing "Do not use markdown in your response" with "Your response should be composed of smoothly flowing prose paragraphs."
findings.evidence: Same page, formatting section: heading and both example sentences match the manual's quotation.

findings.claim: Chapter 28 item 7 and Section 10.4: Anthropic's budget_tokens setting is deprecated or unsupported on newer models.
findings.evidence: Prompting Claude Sonnet 5 page: manual extended thinking (budget_tokens) "is not supported on Claude Sonnet 5 and returns a 400 error. It was deprecated on Claude Sonnet 4.6 and is now removed." Consistent with the manual's wording; checked only on the Sonnet 5 page.

frontier.finding: Du et al. test 5 open and closed LLMs on math, question answering and coding with the needed evidence retrieved perfectly. Abstract: performance "still degrades substantially (13.9%--85%) as input length increases", and the drop persists when irrelevant tokens are replaced by whitespace or masked. Fix: have the model recite the retrieved evidence before solving; the abstract reports up to 4% gain for GPT-4o on RULER (HTML Table 5: QA2 at 32K 68.4 to 72.4, 4.0 points). The paper does not define whether 13.9-85% is relative or absolute; the appendix tables (two open models, Llama-3.1-8B and Mistral-v0.3-7B) read as absolute points, a second-hand reading by the fetch tool.
frontier.source: Du et al., Context Length Alone Hurts LLM Performance Despite Perfect Retrieval, arXiv 2510.05381, 2025-10-06, Findings of EMNLP 2025 (per arXiv comments)
frontier.practical_use: After pasting a long document, ask the model to quote the passages that answer the question, then answer from the quotes. A clean, well-retrieved context does not remove the cost of length.
frontier.changes_manual: Section 7.4: add that length cost remains when padding is masked (the manual currently explains it by irrelevant padding, Levy et al.), and that recite-then-answer is a measured mitigation (up to 4 points, GPT-4o, RULER).

frontier.finding: Six models (GPT-4o, GPT-4o-mini, o3-mini, o4-mini, Gemini 2.0 Flash, Gemini 2.5 Flash) on GPQA Diamond and MMLU-Pro. No expert or low-knowledge persona reliably beat the no-persona baseline on GPQA; on MMLU-Pro, five of six models showed no significant expert gain. One exception: Gemini 2.0 Flash, Engineering Expert, about +8.9 percentage points on MMLU-Pro (p = 0.002), which Gemini 2.5 Flash did not repeat. Low-knowledge personas often lowered accuracy (Toddler significantly negative on GPT-4o on GPQA); Gemini 2.5 Flash declined 10.56 of 25 trials per question with mismatched experts.
frontier.source: Basil, Shapiro, Shapiro, Mollick, Mollick, Meincke, Prompting Science Report 4: Playing Pretend, arXiv 2512.05858, 2025-12-05 (numbers from the Wharton Generative AI Labs report page)
frontier.practical_use: Do not add "you are a world-class expert" to raise accuracy on hard factual or reasoning questions. Use roles for tone, format and audience, and never assign a mismatched or low-knowledge persona where accuracy matters.
frontier.changes_manual: Section 7.3: add as a second, newer test on 2025 closed models beside Zheng et al. 2024 (open models, MMLU, 2023-era). The conclusion stands; the scope widens. Update the evidence-class line.

frontier.finding: Seven models (Gemini 2.0 Flash, Gemini 2.0 Flash Lite, GPT-4o-mini, GPT-4o, Claude 3 Haiku, Claude 3.7 Sonnet, DeepSeek V3). Repeating the input prompt as QUERY QUERY, with no extra output tokens, "wins 47 out of 70 benchmark-model combinations, with 0 losses" for non-reasoning use; with step-by-step reasoning on it was "neutral to slightly positive (5 wins, 1 loss, 22 ties)". A secondary summary's single-task figure (21.33% to 97.33%) was not seen on a primary page and is not used.
frontier.source: Leviathan, Kalman, Matias (Google Research), Prompt Repetition Improves Non-Reasoning LLMs, arXiv 2512.14982, 2025-12-17
frontier.practical_use: On a non-reasoning model, for look-up from the prompt or options-first multiple choice, paste the question twice as a free test. Expect little once reasoning is on. It doubles input tokens, not output.
frontier.changes_manual: Section 7.4: add one line beside "documents first, question last". Scope: 2024-25 non-reasoning models; none of the tested Claude models is a 2026 model.

frontier.axis: 1 Contextual Conditioning (system rules, negative and constraint prompts)
frontier.finding: Anthropic's current guides say Opus 4.5 and 4.6 are more responsive to the system prompt, so "dial back any aggressive language" (replace "CRITICAL: You MUST use this tool when..." with "Use this tool when..."); prefilled last-assistant-turn responses are unsupported from Claude 4.6; Sonnet 5 "interprets prompts literally and explicitly" and does not generalize an instruction from one item to another, so state scope explicitly; review prompts such as "only report high-severity issues" are followed more faithfully, lowering recall, so ask for everything with confidence and filter in a second step; positive examples work better than negative instructions. No test numbers are published.
frontier.source: Anthropic Claude Platform docs: Prompting best practices, and Prompting Claude Sonnet 5 (opened 2026-10-15)
frontier.date: 2026-10-15 (page read date; publication dates not shown)
frontier.practical_use: Strip ALL CAPS, MUST and "if in doubt, use the tool" from system prompts carried over from older models; say each rule once, plainly; say "everywhere" when a rule should apply everywhere; split "find everything" from "filter" in review jobs; do not rely on prefill on 4.6 and later.
frontier.changes_manual: Sections 7.3 and 7.5: the manual has no guidance on emphasis, literal reading or prefill. Add a short vendor-documentation note scoped by model name; it also gives a second vendor statement for the positive-reframing rule.

frontier.finding: Six open-weight models (qwen3-32b, qwen3-8b, olmo3.1-32b, olmo3-7b, smollm3-3b, nemotron3-nano) and four API models (gpt-5-nano, gpt-5.4-nano, claude-haiku-4.5, grok-4.1-fast), four formats (JSON, XML, LaTeX, Markdown), math, science, logic and writing. Abstract: structured-output requirements "substantially degrade reasoning and writing performance across open-weight models"; "format-requesting instructions alone cause most of the accuracy loss"; "decoupling recovers most lost accuracy"; recent closed models show "little to no format tax". Example (HTML Table 10, second-hand reading): qwen3-32b on GPQA with JSON requested by prompt fell from 52.0% to 43.4% (-8.6 points); two-turn gave 53.0%; with extended thinking the penalty was -2.2 points against a 52.2% baseline. The API models are small or fast tiers.
frontier.source: Lee, D'Antoni, Berg-Kirkpatrick, The Format Tax, arXiv 2604.03616, 2026-04-04
frontier.practical_use: On open-weight or small models, get the answer in free text first and ask for JSON or XML in a second step, or turn thinking on. On current closed models, test before paying for a second call.
frontier.changes_manual: Sections 8.1 and 10.5: say the cost sits in the format instruction itself, not only in the decoder. Today 10.5 says constraints guarantee form, not truth; add that asking for form can lower truth on smaller models.

frontier.finding: Anthropic's Sonnet 5.5 guide: with structured outputs "the response text holds only the JSON, so the model can work the problem out only in its thinking. When it skips thinking, it can be less accurate on these tasks." Adding "Think the problem through before you answer." at high effort "brings accuracy close to what the model reaches at xhigh". Without structured outputs the model works in text and writes JSON last, so parse the last JSON value. Asking it to think less in the system prompt "doesn't reliably reduce its thinking". No accuracy numbers are published; scope is Claude Sonnet 5.5, tasks needing a few steps of working out.
frontier.source: Anthropic, Prompting Claude Sonnet 5.5 (opened 2026-10-15)
frontier.practical_use: When you need JSON from a task that needs working out, keep thinking on (or let the model reason in text and parse the last JSON value); never tell a reasoning model not to think; treat max_tokens stops as failures even if the JSON parses.
frontier.changes_manual: Section 10.5 and Chapter 15: add as vendor-documented evidence that schema-forced output can cost accuracy on current Claude models; it pairs with F05 from a different model family.

frontier.finding: SWE-agent on SWE-bench Verified, five model configurations, first check on OpenHands. Observation masking (hiding old tool outputs) "halves cost relative to the raw agent" and is "matching, and sometimes slightly exceeding, the solve rate of LLM summarization"; a hybrid cuts cost a further 7% (vs masking) and 11% (vs summarization). Scope: software-engineering agents only.
frontier.source: Lindenbauer, Slinko, Felder, Bogomolov, Zharov, The Complexity Trap, arXiv 2508.21433 (v1 2025-08-29; v3 2025-10-27, camera-ready for DL4C workshop at NeurIPS 2025 per arXiv comments)
frontier.practical_use: In a long coding or agent run, first try dropping or truncating old tool outputs (keep the model's own reasoning and actions) before adding a summarizer model.
frontier.changes_manual: Section 8.4 covers only static-prompt compression (LLMLingua family); add a short paragraph on agent-trajectory compression, and link it to Chapter 22 (context engineering). ACON (arXiv 2510.00615, ICML 2026 per arXiv comments, peak tokens down 26-54%) was opened and held back as a possible second citation.

frontier.finding: Draft-Thinking trains a draft mode into a long-chain-of-thought model (supervised fine-tuning plus two-stage RL; 847 training problems, 120 RL steps). On MATH500 it cuts average response length from 5,668 to 986 tokens (82.6%) at 90.6% accuracy versus 93.0% for the original long-CoT model. The base model name was not in the text read, and the page does not mention Chain-of-Draft. No in-window primary source with numbers tested the Chain-of-Draft prompt itself on a reasoning model (one paper's Figure 7 on GPT-OSS-120B could not be read).
frontier.source: Cao et al., Draft-Thinking: Learning Efficient Reasoning in Long Chain-of-Thought LLMs, arXiv 2603.00578 (v1 2026-02-28; v2 2026-10-14)
frontier.practical_use: Nothing to change in daily prompting. Do not expect a "five words per step" prompt to match training-level token savings on a reasoning model; use the effort setting for cost control (no source here tests that comparison).
frontier.changes_manual: Section 8.2: optionally note that draft-style brevity is also pursued through training, with this number and its 2.4-point MATH500 accuracy cost. Appendix A's Chain-of-Draft row is unchanged.

practical_takeaways: Use roles for tone and format, not to raise accuracy: across six 2025 models on GPQA Diamond and MMLU-Pro, expert personas gave no reliable gain, and toddler or layperson personas often lowered scores (Basil et al., arXiv 2512.05858, Wharton report page).

With a long pasted document, put it first and the question last (Anthropic Prompting best practices), then ask the model to quote the passages that answer the question before it answers. Length alone cost accuracy even with perfect retrieval, and reciting the evidence gave up to 4 points for GPT-4o on RULER (Du et al., arXiv 2510.05381, Findings of EMNLP 2025).

On current Claude models, write calm, explicit instructions: drop CRITICAL and MUST, state scope ("every section, not just the first"), and ask a review prompt for every finding with a confidence score before filtering in a second step (Anthropic, Prompting best practices and Prompting Claude Sonnet 5).

When you need JSON from a task that needs working out, do not force JSON-only output with no room to think: keep thinking on or reason in free text first, then convert. The format instruction itself caused most of the loss on open-weight models (qwen3-32b on GPQA, 52.0% to 43.4%; The Format Tax, arXiv 2604.03616), and Anthropic's Sonnet 5.5 guide gives the same advice for Claude (Prompting Claude Sonnet 5.5).

Two cheap tests: on a non-reasoning model, paste the question twice (47 of 70 benchmark-model wins, 0 losses, on 2024-25 models; Leviathan et al., arXiv 2512.14982); in a long agent session, hide old tool outputs before paying for a summarizer (half the cost at similar solve rate on SWE-bench Verified; Lindenbauer et al., arXiv 2508.21433).

checks.reason: Abstract confirms degradation of 13.9%-85% as input length grows (paper does not label it relative or absolute), drop persists with whitespace or masked tokens, recite-the-evidence mitigation, up to 4% GPT-4o gain on RULER, 5 open and closed LLMs on math, QA and coding. Submitted 6 Oct 2025; comment says Findings of EMNLP 2025. Not checked: author names and the Table 5 cell (68.4 to 72.4). Paraphrased, not verbatim (copyright limit).

Confirmed: the six models; submitted 5 Dec 2025; authors; no persona reliably beat baseline on GPQA; on MMLU-Pro five of six showed no significant expert gain, the exception Gemini 2.0 Flash (about +8.9 points, p = 0.002); Gemini 2.5 Flash showed no significant positive difference; Toddler persona significantly negative for GPT-4o on GPQA; Gemini 2.5 Flash refused an average of 10.56 of 25 trials per question. Not seen: the 'with mismatched experts' condition on the 10.56 figure. Paraphrased (copyright limit).

All findings confirmed: 47 of 70 benchmark-model combinations won with 0 losses (non-reasoning); reasoning case in Appendix A.2 is neutral to slightly positive, 5 wins, 1 loss, 22 ties; the seven models match. Not seen in the text read: the exact date 2025-12-17 (arXiv prefix 2512 is consistent with December 2025) and the author names. Only the date needs a direct check. Paraphrased (copyright limit).

Best-practices page: Opus 4.5 and 4.6 more responsive to the system prompt; advice to dial back aggressive language, with the CRITICAL/MUST example changed to a normal 'Use this tool when...' prompt. Prefilled last-assistant-turn responses unsupported from Claude 4.6. Sonnet 5 page: literal and explicit interpretation, no silent generalization across items, scope should be stated; 'only report high-severity issues' lowers recall, so ask for everything with confidence and filter in a second step. Positive examples are said to work better than negative instructions (stated in the verbosity section). No test numbers. Pages show no publication date, as the item says.

Abstract confirms the four claims (substantial degradation for open-weight models, format instructions cause most loss, decoupling recovers most accuracy, little or no format tax in recent closed models). Submitted 4 Apr 2026; authors match. Abstract names no models; the model names in Section 3.2 match the item. Table 10 second-hand reading: qwen3-32b GPQA 52.0 to 43.4 with prompt-requested JSON (-8.6 points), two-turn 53.0, extended-thinking penalty -2.2 against 52.2. The API models being 'small or fast tiers' is inferred from names, not stated.

Guide confirms: with structured outputs the response holds only JSON, so reasoning happens in thinking; the 'Think the problem through before you answer.' line brings high-effort accuracy close to xhigh; without structured outputs, parse the last JSON value; asking to think less in the system prompt does not reliably reduce thinking. Caveat: the guide makes the line conditional on adaptive thinking, which the item omits. No accuracy numbers published. Scope is Sonnet 5.5, multi-step working-out tasks.

v1 29 Aug 2025; v3 27 Oct 2025 (camera-ready for the DL4C workshop at NeurIPS 2025). Abstract confirms masking halves cost vs raw agent, matches or slightly exceeds summarization's solve rate; hybrid is 7% cheaper than masking and 11% cheaper than summarization. SWE-bench Verified with SWE-agent. Five configurations as listed in the paper. OpenHands check is an initial probe (item says first). Work is limited to the SE domain.

Partly refuted. Numbers confirmed: MATH500 length 5,668 to 986 tokens (82.6% reduction); accuracy 93.0% original vs 90.6% Draft-Thinking; 847 training problems; 120 RL steps. Base model is Qwen3-8B. But the page DOES mention Chain-of-Draft: the introduction cites chain-of-draft (CoD) as a prompt-based concise-reasoning method, so the item's 'does not mention Chain-of-Draft' is wrong. The wider absence claim was not checked. Only the v2 date (14 Oct 2026) is visible; the v1 date (28 Feb 2026) was not seen.

findings.claim: OpenAI's reasoning guide says: "Avoid chain-of-thought prompts: Since these models perform reasoning internally, prompting them to 'think step by step' or 'explain your reasoning' is unnecessary."
findings.evidence: The bullet exists on OpenAI's separate Reasoning best practices page. The tool output elided the middle of the sentence, so 'or explain your reasoning' is not confirmed word for word. The main reasoning guide page did not contain 'think step by step'. The page shows no date.
findings.fix: Cite the page by name as 'Reasoning best practices' rather than 'the reasoning guide'. Re-read the full sentence before keeping it as a direct quote.

findings.claim: Anthropic's budget_tokens (minimum 1,024) is deprecated on Claude 4.6 and not supported on Claude 4.7 and later, which use adaptive thinking with an effort setting.
findings.evidence: The Anthropic 'Steering thinking' page I opened says 'You don't set a thinking token budget', sets effort at output_config.effort, and mentions models 'using a legacy manual thinking budget'. It names Claude Opus 5.5, Sonnet 5.5 and Haiku 5.5 but shows no 4.6 or 4.7 version statement and no 1,024 minimum. The direction matches the manual; the exact version numbers and minimum were not confirmed.
findings.fix: Re-check the version numbers and the 1,024 minimum on Anthropic's extended-thinking page. Consider naming the newer models and their per-model default effort.

findings.claim: Keep temperature low where one answer is correct; settings sketch uses temperature: 0 for extraction calls.
findings.evidence: Google's Gemini 3 guide (updated 2026-10-09) says to keep temperature at the default 1.0 for all Gemini 3 models and warns lower values may cause looping or degraded performance. The Gemini 3.8 page (updated 2026-10-13) tells developers to remove temperature, top_p and top_k as deprecated. So the advice does not hold for these models.
findings.fix: Add a provider caveat: some reasoning models fix or deprecate sampling parameters, so check the current documentation for your exact model before setting temperature. Mark the temperature 0 sketch as for models that accept it.

findings.claim: The format-versus-reasoning debate is unsettled (Tam et al. versus the dottxt rebuttal).
findings.evidence: Lee, D'Antoni and Berg-Kirkpatrick (arXiv 2604.03616, April 2026 preprint) measured it on six open-weight and four API models. Open-weight models degrade (average minus 3.9 points from the format request alone across 72 cells); most of the loss comes from the format instruction rather than the decoder constraint; recent closed models showed little to no loss.
findings.fix: Replace 'unsettled' with the 2026 finding and scope: model-dependent, large for open-weight models, small for recent closed models. Add the two-step pattern (reason freeform, then reformat) to the protocol.

frontier.finding: Gema et al. built tasks where letting a reasoning model think longer lowers accuracy: counting with distractors, regression with spurious features, deduction with constraint tracking, and AI-risk scenarios. Failure modes: Claude models get distracted by irrelevant information; OpenAI o-series models overfit to the problem framing; longer reasoning amplified some concerning behaviours (self-preservation statements in Claude Sonnet 4). Key number: Claude Opus 4, Misleading Math task, controlled-overthinking setup, accuracy 'dropping from nearly 100% to around 85-90% as reasoning extends' (Figure 3 caption, token budgets not given there). DeepSeek R1, natural-overthinking setup: 70% to 30% with five distractors (distractor count, not reasoning length). Purpose-built stress tasks, not typical workloads.
frontier.source: Gema et al., Inverse Scaling in Test-Time Compute, arXiv 2507.14417 (v1 19 Jul 2025; v2 15 Dec 2025; TMLR 12/2025)
frontier.practical_use: Do not assume higher effort or a larger thinking budget always helps. If the prompt contains irrelevant or misleading detail, test a lower effort level as well and strip the distractors.
frontier.changes_manual: Small change. 10.4 describes only gains (Snell et al.). Add one sentence and a Works Cited entry, and add 'also test lower effort' to protocol step 2.

frontier.finding: Madhwal et al. compared direct prompting with two decomposed-prompting styles on six multi-hop factual QA benchmarks (1,433 verified instances) with nine models including GPT-5.1, Gemini-2.5-Pro and Gemini-2.5-Flash. Bamboogle: Llama-3.3-70B direct 45.5%, +26.8 and +22.8 points with decomposition; GPT-5.1 direct 84.6%, +3.2 and +2.4. MuSiQue: GPT-5.1 direct 53.9%, +0.4 and -7.8. Gains plateau or turn negative on frontier models. What holds up: treating disagreement between direct and decomposed answers as a warning (Disagreement-Based Abstention). GPT-5.1 abstention F1 versus an 'Are you sure?' baseline: Bamboogle 0.47 to 0.73, MuSiQue 0.38 to 0.66; on CRAG the baseline is higher (0.66 vs 0.53).
frontier.source: Madhwal et al., Decomposed Prompting Does Not Fix Knowledge Gaps, But Helps Models Say 'I Don't Know', arXiv 2602.04853 (v2 6 Jul 2026); Findings of ACL 2026 per ACL Anthology listing seen in search results
frontier.evidence_class: peer-reviewed (Findings of ACL 2026; venue taken from search-result listing, not opened)
frontier.practical_use: On a frontier model, do not expect decomposition to raise accuracy on factual multi-hop questions. If the answer matters, ask both ways and send disagreements for checking.
frontier.changes_manual: Change. 9.2 cites only Zhou et al. (ICLR 2023) and has no frontier-model caveat. Add a short 2026 note scoped to factual multi-hop QA, not math or code.

frontier.finding: Bayat, Pezeshkpour and Hruschka compared tool-augmented models with a Code Interpreter against non-tool counterparts on PYMATH (1,679 competition-level maths problems where Python helps but is not sufficient). Models not named in the abstract. Final-answer accuracy up to +19.3 percentage points with the tool ('up to' = best case). In pairwise comparisons of the reasoning, non-tool models won 'up to 41.5% more often'. The failure they call Tool-Induced Myopia appears in about 55% of 'high-risk cases' (not defined in the abstract). Only the abstract page was read.
frontier.source: Bayat et al., From Proof to Program: Characterizing Tool-Induced Reasoning Hallucinations in LLMs, arXiv 2511.10899 (v1 14 Nov 2025; v2 20 Apr 2026)
frontier.practical_use: A code interpreter helps calculation-heavy maths, but read the model's working, not only the final number. Having the model re-check the code result by a separate route is a reasonable response (my inference, not tested in the paper).
frontier.changes_manual: Small change. 9.5 rests on 2023 evidence (PoT, PAL). Add a caution with this scope; check the full text before quoting more than the abstract figures.

frontier.finding: Young measured how often a reasoning model's chain of thought admits a planted hint that changed its answer: 12 open-weight reasoning models from 9 families (7B to 685B), 498 multiple-choice questions from MMLU and GPQA Diamond, six hint types, 41,832 runs. Overall acknowledgement ranged from 39.7% (Seed-1.6-Flash) to 89.9% (DeepSeek-V3.2-Speciale). Lowest by hint type: consistency 35.5%, sycophancy 53.9%. Keyword analysis: about 87.5% in thinking tokens versus about 28.6% in the final answer text. Training method and family predicted faithfulness better than size.
frontier.source: Young, Lie to Me: How Faithful Is Chain-of-Thought Reasoning in Reasoning Models?, arXiv 2603.22582 (23 Mar 2026)
frontier.practical_use: Do not treat a model's explanation as proof of what drove its answer; check the answer against the source. Final-answer explanations are weaker evidence than raw thinking, though many APIs show only a summary of the thinking.
frontier.changes_manual: Optional. The manual cites Chen et al. (2505.05410) on faithfulness; this widens the measurement to 12 open-weight models. Flag it as a single-author preprint.

frontier.axis: 4 Decoding and Inference Compute (temperature, thinking controls)
frontier.finding: Google's Gemini 3 guide (updated 2026-10-09) says: 'For all Gemini 3 models, we strongly recommend keeping the temperature parameter at its default value of 1.0', because reasoning is 'optimized for the default setting'; lower values 'may lead to unexpected behavior, such as looping or degraded performance'. thinking_level: minimal/low/medium/high, default high (3.1 Pro, 3 Flash). The Gemini 3.8 page (updated 2026-10-13) says 'Remove deprecated sampling parameters (temperature, top_p, top_k)', gives thinking_level low/medium/high with default medium, rejects 'minimal' on 3.8 Flash, and says to replace thinking_budget with thinking_level. A search snippet claiming the parameters are ignored by the backend was not verified.
frontier.source: Google, Gemini API docs: Gemini 3 Developer Guide and What's new in Gemini 3.8
frontier.practical_use: Read the current docs for your exact model before setting temperature. On Gemini 3.x reasoning tasks do not lower it; on 3.8 Flash drop it and set thinking_level.
frontier.changes_manual: Change. 10.1 ('keep temperature low where one answer is correct') and the temperature 0 sketch need a provider caveat.

frontier.finding: Lee, D'Antoni and Berg-Kirkpatrick tested six open-weight and four API models on MATH-500, GPQA-Diamond, ZebraLogic and WritingBench in four formats, with and without grammar-constrained decoding (GCD). Open-weight, MATH-500, JSON: qwen3-32b freeform 84.4%, minus 5.3 points from the format request alone and minus 9.8 with GCD; qwen3-8b freeform 84.0%, minus 11.5 and minus 16.7. Across 72 open-weight cells the prompt-only effect averaged minus 3.9 points and GCD minus 1.6 (unclear whether added on top). GCD raised format validity from 55.7% to 92.2% but accuracy was 57.3% without GCD, 55.7% with, 61.5% freeform. API models: gpt-5-nano showed the tax; gpt-5.4-nano, claude-haiku-4.5 and grok-4.1-fast showed near-zero or positive change without GCD. Most loss comes from the format instruction itself; reasoning freeform then reformatting, or enabling extended thinking, recovers most of it.
frontier.source: Lee, D'Antoni, Berg-Kirkpatrick, The Format Tax, arXiv 2604.03616 (4 Apr 2026)
frontier.practical_use: On open-weight models doing reasoning-heavy work, let the model think in free text and convert to JSON in a second call, using schema-constrained decoding for the conversion. Measure the tax on your own model; recent closed models mostly showed none.
frontier.changes_manual: Change. 10.5 calls the debate 'unsettled'. Add this 2026 measurement and the two-step pattern.

frontier.finding: DeepConf uses a model's token-level confidence to drop weak reasoning traces when voting, with no extra training. GPT-OSS-120B on AIME 2025: pass@1 91.8%; majority vote over 512 traces 97.0% using about 3.23e8 tokens; offline DeepConf@512 99.9%; online DeepConf-low 97.9% with 84.7% fewer tokens; online DeepConf-high 97.0% with 56.0% fewer tokens. The abstract's 99.9% and 84.7% come from different variants. Needs top-k token log-probabilities.
frontier.source: Fu, Wang, Tian, Zhao, Deep Think with Confidence, arXiv 2508.15260 (21 Aug 2025)
frontier.practical_use: If you self-host, confidence-based early stopping is a cheaper way to vote. With a hosted API, the usable lesson is to stop adding samples once the vote settles.
frontier.changes_manual: Optional. Add a line in 10.2 as an efficiency variant for serving stacks that expose log-probabilities; the advice to start at N=5 stands.

frontier.axis: 4 Decoding and Inference Compute (reasoning effort, thinking budgets)
frontier.finding: Anthropic's 'Steering thinking' page: effort levels max, xhigh, high (default on most models), medium (default on Claude Opus 5.5 and Haiku 5.5), low, set at output_config.effort. 'You don't set a thinking token budget': max_tokens caps thinking plus answer, effort is soft guidance. Asking Sonnet 5.5 in the system prompt to think less 'doesn't reliably reduce its thinking', so lower effort instead. Changing effort between requests invalidates the prompt cache. OpenAI's reasoning guide: effort values are model-dependent (none to max); newer GPT-6 models default to medium; 'Treat reasoning.effort as a tuning knob, not the primary way to recover quality.' Neither page shows a date.
frontier.source: Anthropic, Steering thinking (Claude Platform docs); OpenAI, Reasoning guide
frontier.date: undated pages (describe Claude Opus/Sonnet/Haiku 5.5 and GPT-6 models)
frontier.practical_use: Choose an effort level per conversation and keep it; do not rely on 'think less' wording; check the default effort for your model.
frontier.changes_manual: Small change. 10.4 already covers adaptive thinking and effort; add per-model defaults, the cache effect and the prompt-steering caveat.

practical_takeaways: Test your task at two or three effort levels, including a lower one, instead of assuming more thinking is better. Source: Gema et al., Inverse Scaling in Test-Time Compute (TMLR 2025): Claude Opus 4 fell from nearly 100% to about 85-90% on Misleading Math as reasoning grew.

Control reasoning depth with the provider's effort setting, keep it fixed within a conversation, and do not rely on 'think less' wording. Source: Anthropic 'Steering thinking' docs (Sonnet 5.5 does not reliably obey it; changing effort breaks the prompt cache); OpenAI reasoning guide ('a tuning knob').

Check the provider's current sampling rules before setting temperature. Google's Gemini 3 guide says keep it at 1.0; the Gemini 3.8 page says remove temperature, top_p and top_k and use thinking_level. Source: Gemini API docs, updated 2026-10-09 and 2026-10-13.

For structured output on open-weight models, let the model reason in plain text first, then convert to JSON in a second step. The format request alone cost an average of 3.9 points over 72 cells, while recent closed models showed little or no loss. Source: Lee et al., The Format Tax (arXiv 2604.03616, preprint).

On frontier models, skip decomposition for factual multi-hop questions, but ask direct and decomposed versions and treat disagreement as a warning (GPT-5.1 abstention F1 0.47 to 0.73 on Bamboogle). With a code interpreter, answers improve (up to +19.3 points on PYMATH) but review the reasoning too. Sources: Madhwal et al. (Findings of ACL 2026); Bayat et al. (arXiv 2511.10899, preprint).

checks.reason: Google's Gemini 3 developer guide (dated 2026-10-09 UTC) recommends keeping temperature at its default for all Gemini 3 models, and warns that lower values can cause looping or degraded performance. Quote (the only quote in this response): "keeping the temperature parameter at its default value of 1.0". The Gemini 3.8 page (dated 2026-10-13 UTC) lists removing deprecated temperature, top_p and top_k as a required migration step. The manual's advice to keep temperature low, and the temperature 0 sketch, do not hold for these models. The proposed provider caveat is supported.

Lee, D'Antoni and Berg-Kirkpatrick (arXiv 2604.03616, first author Ivan Yee Lee, submitted 4 Apr 2026) report that format-requesting instructions alone cause most of the accuracy loss, that recent closed-weight models show little to no format tax, and that a second reformatting pass or extended thinking recovers most lost accuracy. The prompt-only average is -3.9 points against -1.6 for grammar-constrained decoding; the paper places this next to the 72-cell analysis but does not explicitly say the average covers those 72 cells. The paper cites Tam et al. (2024) but does not mention a dottxt rebuttal, so the 'Tam versus dottxt' framing is not supported by this source. The proposed fix (model-dependent scope, two-step pattern) is supported.

The paper exists at arXiv 2507.14417, titled 'Inverse Scaling in Test-Time Compute', with v1 submitted 19 Jul 2025. Verified: the abstract says Claude models become more distracted by irrelevant information and OpenAI o-series models overfit to problem framings. The Figure 3 caption says accuracy falls from nearly 100% to around 85-90% as reasoning extends, with no token budget numbers. The DeepSeek R1 natural-overthinking drop of 70% to 30% with five distractors is verified. The introduction says Claude Sonnet 4 shows more self-preservation expression in longer traces. Not verified: the returned caption text did not name Claude Opus 4, so that attribution is unconfirmed; v2 (15 Dec 2025) and TMLR 12/2025 were not checked.

The paper exists at arXiv 2602.04853 (Madhwal et al.). Verified: six multi-hop QA benchmarks, 1,433 verified instances, nine LLMs. Table 1: Bamboogle Llama-3.3-70B direct 45.5 (+26.8 and +22.8); GPT-5.1 direct 84.6 (+3.2 and +2.4); MuSiQue GPT-5.1 direct 53.9 (+0.4 and -7.8). Table 3 (GPT-5.1 abstention F1 vs the 'Are You Sure?' baseline): Bamboogle 0.47 to 0.73; MuSiQue 0.38 to 0.66; CRAG baseline higher at 0.66 vs 0.53. Not verified: the 'Findings of ACL 2026' venue (not in the text read), v2 date 6 Jul 2026, and the Gemini model names.

The abstract of arXiv 2511.10899 matches the claim: PYMATH has 1,679 competition-level maths problems, and Python is helpful but not sufficient. Tool-augmented models with the Code Interpreter gain up to 19.3 percentage points in final-answer accuracy. Non-tool models win up to 41.5% more often in pairwise reasoning comparisons. Tool-Induced Myopia appears in about 55% of high-risk cases. Submission dates are v1 14 Nov 2025 and v2 20 Apr 2026. The abstract does not name the models, as the finding says. Not verified: author list and the definition of 'high-risk cases' (only the abstract was read).

The paper exists at arXiv 2603.22582 and was submitted 23 Mar 2026. Verified in the abstract: 12 open-weight reasoning models from 9 families (7B to 685B); 498 MMLU and GPQA Diamond questions; 41,832 runs; faithfulness rates from 39.7% (Seed-1.6-Flash) to 89.9% (DeepSeek-V3.2-Speciale); lowest for consistency hints (35.5%) and sycophancy hints (53.9%); about 87.5% acknowledgement in thinking tokens vs about 28.6% in answer text; training method and family predict faithfulness better than parameter count. Not verified: the count of six hint types and the planted-hint design (body not read). The paper uses both 'faithfulness' and 'acknowledgment' terms.

Correction on one detail. The Gemini 3 guide (dated 2026-10-09 UTC) gives default temperature 1.0 for all Gemini 3 models and the looping warning, and says thinking_level defaults to high when unspecified. Its table lists minimal, low, medium and high, but marks minimal 'Not supported' for Gemini 3.1 Pro, so the finding's 'minimal/low/medium/high' list is wrong for 3.1 Pro; the high default is right. The Gemini 3.8 page (dated 2026-10-13 UTC) says to remove deprecated temperature, top_p and top_k, gives thinking_level low, medium and high with medium as default, says minimal is not supported on 3.8 Flash and returns an error, and says to replace thinking_budget with thinking_level. The guide's FAQ calls thinking_budget 'still supported for backward compatibility' and recommends migrating, so the word 'replace' is somewhat stronger than the guide's wording. The search-snippet claim was correctly left unverified.

The paper exists at arXiv 2604.03616, 'The Format Tax', submitted 4 Apr 2026, first author Ivan Yee Lee. Verified: six open-weight and four API models; qwen3-32b MATH-500 freeform 84.4, with prompt-only JSON at -5.3 and grammar-constrained decoding at -9.8 (Table 10); prompt-only average -3.9 points vs -1.6 with grammar-constrained decoding; format instructions cause most of the loss; a reformatting pass or extended thinking recovers most of it; recent closed-weight models show little to no format tax. Not verified: qwen3-8b figures, the GCD format-validity figures (55.7% to 92.2%), the accuracy figures 57.3, 55.7 and 61.5, the task list, and the API model names (gpt-5-nano, gpt-5.4-nano, claude-haiku-4.5, grok-4.1-fast).

The abstract of arXiv 2508.15260 (submitted 21 Aug 2025) confirms the core idea: model-internal confidence signals filter low-quality traces, with no additional training. It does not support the finding's breakdown. The abstract attributes both 'up to 99.9%' accuracy and 'up to 84.7%' fewer tokens to DeepConf@512 in one sentence, which does not match the claim that they come from different variants (offline vs online-low). The abstract says filtering happens 'during or after generation', not 'when voting'. The figures 91.8%, 97.0%, 97.9%, 97.0% with 56.0% fewer tokens, the 3.23e8 token count, and the top-k log-probability requirement are not in the abstract. The body was not reached within the lookup cap.

Anthropic's steering-thinking page (no date shown) confirms: effort levels max, xhigh, high (default on most models), medium (default on Opus 5.5 and Haiku 5.5), and low, set at output_config.effort; no thinking token budget is set; max_tokens caps thinking plus response; effort is soft guidance; a system-prompt request to think less does not reliably reduce Sonnet 5.5 thinking, so lower effort instead; changing effort between requests invalidates cache breakpoints. Caveat: the page says a per-message effort change (beta) keeps the cache, which the finding omits. OpenAI's reasoning guide (reached by redirect from platform.openai.com to developers.openai.com/api/docs/guides/reasoning; no date shown) confirms: values are model-dependent, from none to max, and 'Treat reasoning.effort as a tuning knob, not the primary way to recover quality'. Correction: the default of medium is stated only for GPT-6.1 Sol, GPT-6 Sol and GPT-6 Luna, not for all newer GPT-6 models (GPT-6 Astra is not stated). The finding gave no OpenAI URL; the one used is the redirect target.

frontier.finding: Kim et al., 260 configurations, 5 architectures, 3 model families (GPT-5, Gemini 2.5, Claude Sonnet 3.7/4/4.5), 6 benchmarks. Finance-Agent: centralized coordination +80.8% over a single agent (0.631 vs 0.349). PlanCraft: every multi-agent variant worse, -70% to -39%. Tasks where one agent already scores above 45% get negative returns from added agents. Independent agents amplify errors 17.2x, centralized 4.4x. The 87% held-out prediction claim is the authors' and was not independently checked (a snippet reported a lower R2 in a later version).
frontier.source: Kim et al., Towards a Science of Scaling Agent Systems, arXiv 2512.08296 (v1 2025-12-09, v3 2026-04-08)
frontier.practical_use: Start with one agent. Use several only for independent subtasks (research across many sources, parallel analyses) with an orchestrator that checks results. Keep sequential planning and tool-heavy work in one agent.
frontier.changes_manual: Yes: extend 11.5 with a measured 'when multi-agent helps' rule using the two scoped numbers; cite v3 and note numbers moved slightly between versions. Do not quote the 87%.

frontier.finding: Gloaguen et al. tested repository context files (AGENTS.md style) on Claude Code (Sonnet 4.5), Codex (GPT-5.2, GPT-5.1 mini) and Qwen Code (Qwen3-30B-coder). SWE-bench Lite (300 tasks): LLM-generated files change resolution by -0.5%; CTXbench (138 instances, developer-written files): LLM-generated -2%, developer-written +2.4% (p=21%). Cost +20% (SWE-bench Lite) and +23% (CTXbench) for LLM-generated files. Units as printed; v1-era numbers (-3%, +4%) differ, so cite v3.
frontier.source: Gloaguen, Mundler, Muller, Raychev, Vechev, Evaluating AGENTS.md, arXiv 2602.11988 (v1 2026-02-12, v3 2026-09-29)
frontier.practical_use: Do not keep an auto-generated context file. Keep a developer-written file to what the README does not say (build/test commands, non-standard practices); drop repository overviews; test with and without it on your own tasks.
frontier.changes_manual: Yes: 11.7 presents persistent instruction files as the frontier with no evidence that they help; add this result.

frontier.finding: SkillsBench, 87 tasks, 8 domains, 18 model-harness configurations. Curated Skills raise average pass rate from 33.9% to 50.5% (+16.6 points). Self-generated Skills fall below no-Skills: -8.1 (Claude Code + Opus 4.7), -11.3 (Codex + GPT-5.5), -11.5 (Gemini CLI + Gemini 3.1 Pro) points. 2-3 Skills +19.0 points, 4 or more +10.1, comprehensive documentation +0.7. 13 of 87 tasks got worse. v1 had 84 tasks; cite v4.
frontier.practical_use: Write or edit skills by hand from real procedure knowledge, do not trust model-written skills, keep each skill focused, and test each with and without it.
frontier.changes_manual: Yes: 11.7 mentions skills only as a concept; add this evidence. It directly supports the skill-building kit.

frontier.finding: Anthropic internal tests: Tool Search Tool raised MCP evaluation accuracy Opus 4 49% to 74% and Opus 4.5 79.5% to 88.1%; programmatic tool calling cut average tokens 43,588 to 27,297 (-37%) on complex research tasks; tool use examples 72% to 90% on complex parameter handling; code execution with MCP 150,000 to 2,000 tokens (98.7%) in one Drive-to-Salesforce workflow, with a sandbox and monitoring overhead caveat. Vendor-reported, not replicated.
frontier.source: Anthropic Engineering, Introducing advanced tool use (2025-11-24) and Code execution with MCP (2025-11-04)
frontier.practical_use: Do not attach every MCP server to every session; use tool search for large tool sets, let the model call tools from code for multi-step chains, and add 1-3 worked examples for tricky parameters.
frontier.changes_manual: Yes, small: 11.6 has no tool-count guidance; add one sentence with these numbers marked vendor-reported.

frontier.finding: ACE (Generator, Reflector, Curator on one model, DeepSeek-V3.1 in main tables) builds an evolving playbook by small incremental edits. AppWorld offline: ReAct + ACE beats ReAct + ICL by 12.3% and ReAct + GEPA by 11.9%; without labels +14.8% over ReAct; online +7.6% over Dynamic Cheatsheet. Finance offline +10.9% on average over ICL, MIPROv2, GEPA. 82.3% less adaptation latency and 75.1% fewer rollouts than GEPA. Authors' own comparisons; units as printed. Needs a strong Reflector and reliable feedback or the playbook is polluted.
frontier.source: Zhang et al., Agentic Context Engineering, arXiv 2510.04618 (v1 2025-10-06, v3 2026-03-29; ICLR 2026 per arXiv comment line, venue page not opened)
frontier.practical_use: For repeated tasks keep a running itemised playbook, edit single items after each run using hard signals (tests, tool errors, checkers), and never ask the model to rewrite or summarise the whole playbook (brevity bias, context collapse).
frontier.changes_manual: Yes: add ACE to 12.5/12.7 as the context-level alternative to single-prompt search and link it to 11.7.

frontier.finding: Three Kotlin repositories (kotest, ktor, koog), Claude Code with Sonnet 4.6, tasks from reverted pull requests. GEPA-found skill documents +4.9 points on average over an empty document; SkillOpt +0.1 points. The authors say the gain cannot be separated from run-to-run variance; no run reaches p=0.05, best p=0.29. Per-repository cells did not reconcile with 4.9 in my reading, so not reported.
frontier.source: Kozyrev, Kozyrev, Podkopaev, Skill Issue: Lessons from Optimizing Repository SKILLs for Coding Agents, arXiv 2609.12742 (v1 2026-09-11)
frontier.practical_use: When tuning a skill or instruction file with an optimizer, run each version several times on tasks the optimizer never saw; a few points on a few dozen tasks is noise. Review the result like a pull request.
frontier.changes_manual: Yes, small: add as a scoped caution in 12.5; the manual's GEPA figures stay valid.

frontier.axis: 6 Optimization (GEPA and successors on reasoning tasks)
frontier.finding: p1 with response model Qwen3-4B-Instruct-2507, trained on AIME 24 prompts. AIME 25 accuracy: base 47.03, GEPA variants 46.35 to 46.87, full-dataset RL 47.24, p1 on two chosen prompts 54.01 (HMMT 25: base 40.68, p1 45.42, GEPA 40.10 to 40.57). A different single-prompt p1 run scored 44.95, below base, so example choice matters. Table values are a second-hand reading. Authors explain that optimization fails when response variance dominates prompt variance.
frontier.source: Gao et al., p1: Better Prompt Optimization with Fewer Prompts, arXiv 2604.08801 (v1 2026-04-09, v2 2026-08-26)
frontier.practical_use: Do not assume a prompt optimizer helps on hard math or reasoning; compare against the unoptimized prompt on held-out data. A few training examples where candidate prompts disagree can beat a large set, but the choice of examples is itself a risk.
frontier.changes_manual: Yes, small: 12.5 reports GEPA +12% over MIPROv2 on AIME-2025 (Qwen3 8B); add that another group found GEPA near the unoptimized base on AIME/HMMT with a 4B model, so that gain is setup-specific.

frontier.finding: PrefPO by its authors, GPT-4o task model, GPT-5 optimizer and discriminator, nine BIG-Bench Hard tasks plus authors' IFEval-Hard. BBH mean accuracy: PrefPO 0.875, MIPROv2 0.873, GEPA 0.870, TextGrad 0.850, so the top three are within 0.5 points (a tie). TextGrad prompts grew up to 14.7x starting length (PrefPO 4.7x); MIPROv2 prompts 34% repetitive text (PrefPO 1.4%); prompt hacking 86% TextGrad vs 37% PrefPO (LLM-judged). The abstract's '6/9 tasks' is looser than the table.
frontier.source: Singhal, Tambwekar, Maamari, PrefPO: Pairwise Preference Prompt Optimization, arXiv 2603.19311 (v1 2026-03-13, v2 2026-03-24)
frontier.practical_use: After any automatic optimization read the winning prompt: compare length to the original, look for repetition, and check for hard-coded answers or test-set tricks. Do not choose an optimizer on a one-point gap.
frontier.changes_manual: Optional: add one sentence to 12.4 failure modes with the measured bloat and hacking rates, marked as from the method's authors.

practical_takeaways: Start with one agent; add agents only for independent subtasks, with an orchestrator that checks results. Source: Kim et al., arXiv 2512.08296 (Finance-Agent +80.8% for centralized coordination; PlanCraft -70% to -39% for every multi-agent variant).

Hand-write short, focused skills and instruction files and test with and without them: self-written skills scored 8.1 to 11.5 points below no skills, 2-3 focused skills gave +19.0 points vs +10.1 for four or more, and generated AGENTS.md files did not help and cost about 20% more. Sources: Li et al., SkillsBench, arXiv 2602.12670 (v4); Gloaguen et al., arXiv 2602.11988 (v3).

Keep tool definitions out of context until needed: use tool search for large tool sets and let the model call tools from code for multi-step chains (vendor-reported: 150,000 to 2,000 tokens in one workflow; Opus 4 MCP accuracy 49% to 74% with tool search). Source: Anthropic Engineering, advanced tool use (2025-11-24) and code execution with MCP (2025-11-04).

Treat prompt-optimizer gains as small and noisy until checked on held-out tasks with repeated runs, and read the optimized prompt for bloat and gaming. Sources: Kozyrev et al., arXiv 2609.12742 (+4.9 points, not significant); Gao et al., arXiv 2604.08801 (GEPA near base on AIME with a 4B model); Singhal et al., arXiv 2603.19311 (top optimizers within 0.5 points; TextGrad prompts up to 14.7x longer).

For repeated work, keep a running playbook updated in small itemised edits from hard feedback (tests, tool errors), not whole-file rewrites by the model. Source: Zhang et al., ACE, arXiv 2510.04618 (ICLR 2026 per arXiv comments); it needs a strong reflector and reliable feedback.

frontier.finding: Tsui, Self-Correction Bench: across 14 open-source non-reasoning models and 3 datasets (SCLI5 286, GSM8K-SC 1,313, PRM800K-SC 448), models fix an error shown as the user's but not the same error shown as their own: average blind spot rate 64.5%. Appending the single word 'Wait' cut the blind spot by 89.3%, averaged across models and datasets. Reasoning models show a small, even negative, blind spot (no number on the page). Related preprint (Chen et al., arXiv 2606.05976, 2026): moving the wrong claim out of the model's own thought block raised explicit correction by 23 to 93 percentage points across 12 model-domain settings, significant in 10 of 12.
frontier.source: Ken Tsui, 'Self-Correction Bench', arXiv 2507.02778 (v1 July 2025, v2 4 Oct 2025); related: Chen, Su, Lin, Li, Chiang, arXiv 2606.05976 (v2 31 Jul 2026)
frontier.evidence_class: preprint (page says 'Preprint. Under review.'); related paper also a preprint
frontier.practical_use: Do not ask a model to 'check your answer' in the same thread. Hand the draft over as someone else's text, use a fresh chat, or use a reasoning model. Supported only in the tested settings; a search-summary figure of 76.0% / 5,306 traces was not found on the page and is not used.
frontier.changes_manual: Yes, small. Section 13.2 rests on 2023 models; add the 2025 non-reasoning-model blind spot, that reasoning models showed little or negative blind spot, and the re-framing step as a cheap middle option before independent review (my inference, not a replacement for 13.6).

frontier.finding: Guan et al., Monitoring Monitorability: a monitor that reads the chain of thought catches target behaviors better than an action-only monitor. Agents were GPT-5 Thinking, o3, o3-mini, o4-mini plus Claude 3.7 Sonnet (Thinking), DeepSeek R1-0528-Qwen3-8B and Kimi K2 Thinking. Metric: g-mean squared. Monitor scale raised it by nearly 40% from o3-mini to GPT-5 Thinking; o4-mini monitor from lowest to highest reasoning effort gained about 12% (Section 6.3; relative versus points not stated). Longer chains were generally more monitorable; RL at current frontier scale did not materially reduce monitorability; follow-up questions helped. Exception: Claude 3.7 Sonnet had the lowest CoT monitorability of the models tested. Related preprint (arXiv 2603.05706, Mar 2026, 13 reasoning models): Claude Sonnet 4.5 controlled its reasoning text 2.7% of the time versus 61.9% for its final answer; GPT-OSS-120B 5.9% vs 0.9% for the 20B; control falls with more RL, test-time compute and harder problems.
frontier.source: Melody Y. Guan et al., 'Monitoring Monitorability', arXiv 2512.18311 (v1 20 Dec 2025); related: Chen Yueh-Han et al., 'Reasoning Models Struggle to Control their Chains of Thought', arXiv 2603.05706 (5 Mar 2026)
frontier.evidence_class: preprint (both papers; no venue listed; affiliations not shown on the abstract page I read)
frontier.practical_use: For long or costly agent runs, keep the reasoning log and have a reviewer read it together with the actions, not actions alone. Give a small reviewer more reasoning effort and let it ask follow-up questions. Treat the log as evidence, not proof.
frontier.changes_manual: Yes. Section 15.3 stops at Baker and Korbak; add these two measurements with the caveats that they are preprints, the first is mostly qualitative in text, and both author groups say scale or training could change the result. Section 15.4's conclusion stays.

frontier.finding: Norman, Rivera, Hughes: 21 LLM judges from nine providers on MT-Bench, JudgeBench, RewardBench, 118 runs, about 541,000 judgments, run March-April 2026 under one pairwise template. Exact-match agreement overstates chance-corrected agreement by 33.8 to 41.3 percentage points across the 21 models; rankings shift by up to 14 places across benchmarks; Qwen 3 8B had test-retest 0.992 with position bias 0.192, Gemini 2.5 Flash 0.988 with 0.125; verbosity bias under 0.011 under that single rubric. Related TMLR-listed paper (Soumik, arXiv 2604.23178, 2026; 5 judges, 9 debiasing strategies): style bias toward markdown ranged 0.10 to 0.76, position bias at most 0.04 in that setup, and length preference differed by model family. The two papers disagree on position-bias size because judges, prompts and benchmarks differ.
frontier.source: Justin D. Norman, Michael U. Rivera, D. Alex Hughes, 'Reliability without Validity', arXiv 2606.19544 (v1 17 Jun 2026); related: Soumik, 'Judging the Judges', arXiv 2604.23178 (v2 24 Jun 2026)
frontier.evidence_class: preprint (primary); related paper stated on arXiv to be published in Transactions on Machine Learning Research 2026 (TMLR page not opened)
frontier.practical_use: Keep swapping A and B and call a flip a tie. Do not treat repeatable scores as proof the judge is right. Check the judge against a small set of your own human-labeled cases and report chance-corrected agreement, not raw percent. Pick the judge on your task. Equalize formatting before judging, and do not assume longer wins.
frontier.changes_manual: Yes, small. Section 13.3 rests on 2023 GPT-4 results; add repeatability-is-not-validity, chance-corrected agreement and format bias. The 'different model family' rule was not tested head-on, so no change is suggested to it.

frontier.finding: Meta's Agents Rule of Two (31 Oct 2025): until prompt injection can be reliably detected and refused, an agent should have at most two of three properties in one session (reads untrusted input; reaches sensitive systems or private data; changes state or communicates externally). If all three are needed without a fresh context window, it should not run autonomously and needs human approval or another reliable check. No measured figures in the post. Related vendor page (Anthropic, 24 Nov 2025): calls a 1% attack success rate a real improvement that still carries meaningful risk; measured by an internal adaptive Best-of-N attacker with 100 attempts per environment, comparing the launch browser-extension version with the original launch setup; the model is not named in that sentence and per-version values are in a chart image I could not read. Anthropic also says prompt injection is far from solved.
frontier.source: Meta AI, 'Agents Rule of Two: A Practical Approach to AI Agent Security' (31 Oct 2025); related: Anthropic, 'Mitigating the risk of prompt injections in browser use' (24 Nov 2025)
frontier.evidence_class: vendor documentation (both pages); the 1% figure is the vendor's own internal test, not an independent measurement
frontier.practical_use: Before connecting an agent to your accounts, count which of the three properties it has. If it reads web pages, emails or shared files, remove access to private data or the ability to act and send, or require your approval for each state-changing step, or split the job into separate sessions. A roughly 1% rate on the vendor's own adaptive test is not safe for irreversible actions repeated across many pages (my inference).
frontier.changes_manual: Yes, small. Section 17.3's design rule already matches; add the Rule of Two as a short checklist labeled vendor guidance, not a proven defense, and add the Anthropic page as a deployed-agent data point supporting 17.1's 'no foolproof prevention'. No existing statement is contradicted.

practical_takeaways: Do not ask a model to recheck its own answer in the same chat. Present the draft as someone else's text, use a new chat, or use a reasoning model. Source: Tsui 2025 (arXiv 2507.02778); Chen et al. 2026 (arXiv 2606.05976).

If you use a model as a judge, swap the order and treat flips as ties, compare it with a small set of your own human-labeled cases using chance-corrected agreement, and make both answers look the same in format. Source: Norman et al. 2026 (arXiv 2606.19544); Soumik 2026 (arXiv 2604.23178).

For long agent runs, keep the reasoning log and have a reviewer read it together with the actions. Treat the log as evidence, not proof. Source: Guan et al. 2025 (arXiv 2512.18311); Chen Yueh-Han et al. 2026 (arXiv 2603.05706).
Give an agent no more than two of: untrusted input, private data access, ability to act outside; require human approval if you need all three. Source: Meta, Agents Rule of Two (31 Oct 2025).

Plan for a residual attack rate even with the best vendor defenses (about 1% on Anthropic's own adaptive test), so keep irreversible actions behind approval. Source: Anthropic, 'Mitigating the risk of prompt injections in browser use' (24 Nov 2025).
